name: Grand Wizzard Theodore
hook: Stopped a record with his hand while his mother told him off, heard the noise it made, and turned an accident into a technique the world now recognises instantly.
blurb: Theodore Livingston was twelve, playing records loudly in his bedroom, when his mother came in to tell him to turn it down. He kept his hand on the record while she talked, rubbing it back and forth, and heard the noise that makes. After she left he decided it was worth keeping, practised it, and brought it out at a party. That noise is the scratch, and it is now probably the single most recognisable sound in recorded music. Scratching turned the turntable from something that plays a record into an instrument you can attack and shape, a change in kind, not just in style. He was very young and the setting was a family home: the technique was not developed in a studio or by anyone being paid, and its origin story is a boy being told off. Accounts differ on the year, most giving 1975 and some 1977.
signatureTracksNote: Known for a turntable technique, the scratch, rather than for records of his own.
